steps.title: In the ground
steps.text: Molybdenum occurs as molybdenite (MoS₂), a soft grey sulphide, in the same porphyry deposits that hold most of the world's copper. A few mines dig it for its own sake; much of the rest is a by-product of copper mining.

steps.title: Mine and float
steps.text: Ore is mined from open pits and floated. At copper mines the first float carries copper and molybdenum together; a second float then sinks the copper and lifts the molybdenite on its own.
steps.india: No mine output; depends on imports.

steps.title: Roast
steps.text: The concentrate is roasted in air at about 600°C in a multi-level furnace. Sulphur burns off and leaves technical molybdenum oxide, the form in which most molybdenum is traded.
out: Rhenium, caught from the roaster gas
Sulphur dioxide, captured as sulphuric acid

steps.title: Make
steps.text: Most oxide is added straight to steel furnaces as briquettes, or first reduced with iron into ferromolybdenum. A smaller share is purified into chemicals: catalysts, lubricants and pure metal powder.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: Molybdenum makes steel stronger and harder at high temperature and helps stainless steel resist corrosion. Oil refineries use it in the catalysts that strip sulphur from fuel.
steps.india: Steel and about 249 Mt a year of oil refining create the demand.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Molybdenum returns inside alloy and stainless steel scrap. Spent refinery catalysts are a separate, rich source and are processed for their molybdenum, vanadium and nickel.
out: Spent catalysts also yield vanadium and nickel
steps.india: Rubamin recovers about 1,500 t/yr of molybdenum from spent catalysts.
